note:
The estate's history as a timeline. The spine of it is retold in this record's own words from the concise history printed on The Park Map, Fourth Edition, by Dougal de Havilland, which he gave to the Nottingham Park Residents' Association; the raw transcript stays in history_park_map_dougal.json, where the wording IS his. Entries carrying a source came from elsewhere and are retold on the same terms — nobody's prose is reproduced.

Where the map and the University of Nottingham's archive disagree on a date, the archive is followed, on A. Hagues's instruction: they hold the Newcastle family papers. Every such change keeps a 'corrected' note naming the map's date, so nothing is quietly overwritten. Two of them want a second look — 1087 for the castle, where 1068 is the conventional date and William the Conqueror died in 1087; and 1939 for the sale to Oxford, where the map and the Estate's own history both say 1938.
source: The Park Map, Fourth Edition, designed by Dougal de Havilland and donated to the Nottingham Park Residents' Association. Retold, not reproduced.

entries.text: Saxon settlers arrive and pass the sandstone rock by, putting their settlement instead on the ground where St Mary's church and the Lace Market stand today.

The first castle on the rock is begun. Over the centuries that follow it becomes the chief royal residence of the Midlands, and the woodland beside it is held as a royal park — deer, fish ponds and a rabbit warren, food and sport for whoever held the castle.
entries.corrected: Dougal's map dates this 1068 and credits William the Conqueror, ordering it built by his son Peverel.

entries.text: Henry II, a king said to be immoderate in his love of hunting, adds a falconry to the park.
Nottingham receives its Great Charter, and from this point answers to nobody below the King.
Richard III is said to have mustered his troops in the Deer Park, marching them over the King's Meadow and away to Bosworth.
James I grants the castle and its park to the Earl of Rutland.
Charles I stays at Thurland Hall rather than the castle, which by now is reckoned unfit for a king.

Charles raises his standard on the ground now called Standard Hill. The town stays loyal to Parliament. William Cavendish backs the King heavily, with money and with men; the war ends with Charles executed in 1649.
With Parliament holding the castle, the park's trees are felled to keep the garrison in fuel and timber.
Parliament orders the castle pulled down, to the considerable relief of a good many Nottinghamians.
The ruin and the park are bought by William Cavendish, 1st Duke of Newcastle upon Tyne, made Duke for the support he gave the King in the war. He restocks the park with deer.
The 1st Duke begins an Italianate palace on the castle site, at a cost of £14,000. He dies before it is finished.
The palace is completed — the building that stands on the rock today.

Queen Anne, second daughter of James II, comes to the throne. As Princess Anne she had lived at the Mansion House. Queen Anne's Garden and Queen Anne's Chamber still carry her name at the castle, which suggests she may have been the last of the Stuarts to stay there.
The Duke leaves no male heir, and the title is recreated for his nephew Thomas Pelham, later Pelham-Holles, as 1st Duke of Newcastle.
The park's herd of deer is sold off.
The old deer park is given over to grazing cattle.
No male heir again. The dukedom is recreated a second time, for the nephew Henry Pelham Clinton, who becomes the 2nd Duke.

The last of the great balls is held at the ducal mansion, given by the Duke — Earl of Lincoln and Colonel of the Nottingham Militia as well. The building is then let out as apartments, and in part as a boarding school.
The 2nd Duke gives an acre of the park for the building of Nottingham General Hospital.

The old castle fishponds are filled in with spoil dug out for the Cavalry Barracks going up at the north-west corner of the Park. The made ground, known afterwards as the Fishpond Gardens, is let out in plots and gives allotments with a name for what they grow.
The Cavalry Barracks are built.
Henry Clinton dies and his son Thomas succeeds as 3rd Duke.

The 3rd Duke dies at forty-two, after a whooping cough treatment that went badly wrong. He leaves a widow of thirty-five as Dowager Duchess, and a son of ten — Henry Pelham Fiennes Pelham Clinton, the Fiennes said “fines”.
A riding school is built for the Nottingham Troop of Yeomanry Cavalry.

The Dowager Duchess begins to weigh selling the castle and park. Her agents talk her out of a single sale — it would drag down land values across Nottingham, they say — and advise letting small plots go at the edges instead, a little at a time.
The Dowager marries again, and sells land on Standard Hill to provide for the young Duke.
The first national census puts Nottingham at close to thirty thousand people. It passes forty thousand by 1821, and fifty thousand by 1831.

Thirty-two lots on Standard Hill are sold for building. In the same year the 4th Duke, twenty-two years old, marries the heiress Georgina Elizabeth Munday of Shipley in Derbyshire, and £190,000 with her.
William Stretton builds St James's Church on Standard Hill. A nurses' home will replace it in 1936.
The first house in the park proper goes up opposite the castle gatehouse: the vicarage to St Mary's.
Regency House is built at 2 Ropewalk, and is the oldest house standing in The Park today.

The 4th Duke, who is not popular, sets about developing the edge of the Park and engages the architect John Jephson. The work is never begun. The townspeople resent the whole idea: they regard the Park as their own ground, to walk in.
Jephson is replaced by Peter Frederick Robinson.
Robinson publishes his Plan of Nottingham Park, setting out the intended streets on a grid.
The first houses go up on Park Terrace.
Rioters set the Duke's mansion alight, provoked by his vote against the Reform Bill.
Forty to fifty houses now stand, built in the face of local opposition — on Western Terrace, Park Terrace, and Ropewalk Street, now The Ropewalk.
entries.corrected: Dougal's map puts fifty houses at 1834.

entries.text: Houses begin to appear in the Park proper, inside the old park rather than around its rim.
A visitors' guide of the day describes the Park as open to the public and walked by every class of person — a healthy thing, it says, for a crowded town to have.
The 4th Duke dies. His son, Lord Lincoln, is held in far better regard by the town and its council than his father ever was.

The 5th Duke appoints Thomas Chambers Hine surveyor of the Newcastle estates, with the Park his particular charge. Every house built here must have his approval, including those of his rival Fothergill Watson.
entries.corrected: Dougal's map places Hine's appointment at 1851, with the 4th Duke's death.

entries.text: The Park Tunnel opens — Hine's work, cut to bring carriages down from Derby Road.
Houses stand finished on Castle Grove, Lenton Road, Newcastle Drive and Clinton Terrace.
Hine's dumbbell layout of the Park is established — the double loop of roads the estate still runs on.
The 5th Duke dies and the estate passes to a trust. Hine stays on as its architect.
Around thirty houses go up to Watson Fothergill's designs.
T. C. Hine oversees the restoration of the burnt mansion.
The Midland Counties Art Museum opens inside the castle — the first municipal museum and art gallery in England.

Nearly four hundred houses have been built, for the most part for wealthy and influential Nottingham men: A. J. Mundella the educationalist, Sir Jesse Boot the pharmacist, Sir Albert Ball the plumber, John Player in tobacco, Thomas Foreman the printer, Sir John Jardine in lace machinery, and the Bowden, Birkin and Bayley families — bicycles, lace and leather.
Hine retires, after thirty-seven years with the say over every house on the estate.
Queen Victoria makes Nottingham a city, in the year of her Diamond Jubilee.
The estate is all but finished, at 355 houses.
The riding school is demolished.

The bigger houses are proving hard to sell and many leases are nearly run out. St Heliers, Jesse Boot's old house, empty ten years and said to be sound, goes to auction in June. A jobbing builder from Wilford buys it for £7 — against a ground rent to the Newcastle estate office of £116 a year.
After almost three hundred years, the 8th Duke sells the Park to Oxford University, the purchase made through Lord Nuffield. It is managed for the university's Chest by a firm of London solicitors.
entries.corrected: Dougal's map and the Estate's own history both date the sale 1938.

entries.text: The Oxford University Chest begins selling the freeholds. All the properties had been leasehold on ninety-nine year terms; by 1986 every freehold has gone.
Clumber Park is sold to the National Trust. The house there had been pulled down in 1938 to raise money.
The Park is designated a Conservation Area.

Negotiations that have run for years come good: the Residents' Association takes the estate out of Oxford's hands, and a company limited by guarantee is formed to run it — The Nottingham Park Estate Limited. Years of work by the Association, with the lawyer John Hallam at the helm, stand behind it. The estate is freehold now but still private, and the company takes on the roads, footpaths and common ground.

The gas lighting passes from the Residents' Association to the company. The new directors' list of troubles is a short one and a familiar one: the road surfaces, the through traffic cutting past the ring road, and a Park that has become something close to an inner-city car park.

Residents vote on the street lighting. The Victorian gas lamps are past a hundred years old and have had little attention, and the choice is to keep them or go over to electricity. Keeping them wins by a landslide — 150 lamps at the time. The Park's is now reckoned the largest connected network of gas lamps in the country: London and Malvern have more lamps, but not joined up as these are.
The 10th Duke dies and the dukedom of Newcastle becomes extinct.

The Local Government Finance Act 1988 sweeps away the rating system from April 1990, and with it the company's income. It had been funded by taking fifteen per cent of the General Municipal Rate — a share that existed because Nottingham had charged Park properties fifteen per cent less than others, to allow for what Oxford spent maintaining the estate. That arrangement rested on the Nottingham Borough Extension Act 1877.

The company puts a Bill through Parliament and it becomes law in April: the Nottingham Park Estate Act. It gives the company legal power to raise money — the Park Rates, as they are known here — for the roads, pavements, gas lamps, trees and green spaces including Newcastle and Lincoln Circus, paid on top of council tax. Section 14 covers stopping up roads and regulating traffic. The company is run by an employed Estate Manager under as many as ten resident directors, unpaid volunteers elected by the members at an annual general meeting.

entries.text: The estate's records are moved from Oxford to the University of Nottingham.
